say: Every roof loses sun to something.
A stair room. A water tank. The floor next door. A tree.
And how much it loses decides whether solar is worth it.
Before going solar, a household needs four answers.
Where can panels actually fit?
What shades them, and when?
How much will they make?
And what will it really cost, after the subsidy?
Today, those answers come from a site visit and a round of quotes, and the household can't check any of them.
home sol answers all four, from one tap on a map.
Here's a home in Chundeegarh, in Google's own photo of the street. One tap, on its roof.

It measures the roof from Google's 3D survey: flat, two hundred and twenty-five square metres, about two floors up, and it finds everything around that could cast a shadow. That's geometry, not guesswork.
Then Claude, on Amazon Bedrock, names what was measured: a large cluster of trees to the south-west, a stair room. It can name things. It can't change a measurement.
Next, it runs the sun across the year, every half hour, over those heights, and charges each hour of lost sunlight to whatever blocked it.
The trees take fifty-six percent. On the shortest day, the panel spots are clear of shadow only from about ten until noon.
Panels go only where the sun is good. There's room for twenty-eight, in rows spaced so they don't shade each other in winter.
Say this household uses three hundred and fifty units a month, about nineteen hundred rupees.

The plan: six panels, three point three kilowatts, covering all of it. After the seventy-eight thousand rupee P M Surya Ghar subsidy, it costs one laakh twenty thousand, and pays back in about five years.
And every figure says where it came from: the survey's date, the subsidy rules, the household's own rate.
Now, a what-if: what about five kilowatts? A Strands agent on Claude answers from this plan, using the same finance code as the dashboard.
The bigger system would take about nine years to pay back, not five, because the extra units would earn nothing.
Across eighty-one test questions, seven hundred and eighty-nine of seven hundred and ninety automatic checks passed, and every money figure traced back to the plan's own numbers.
One tap. A measured roof, a year of shadows, a panel plan and an honest price, before the first site visit.
That's home sol.
